ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> All participants provided informed consent.

> Additionally, participants were asked to voluntarily provide complementary demographic information, including their gender, age, baseline frequency of AI use, employment sector, education level, and previous experience with AI-related training.

> Previous AI-training experience indicated whether participants had previously completed at least one AI-related course or training program.

> Due to the small number of participants who did not identify as either male or female, these participants were excluded from the MANCOVA.

> This raises the possibility of selective retention, when more motivated SME participants were more likely to remain in the study, potentially contributing to the comparatively smaller decline in intention to use GenAI observed in this sector.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: AI-literacy training may facilitate workplace adoption of GenAI, yet little is known about how employees' motivational beliefs change during training.
Drawing on expectancyvalue theory, we examined motivation before and after Hazlo con IA, a national adaptive AI-literacy program in Chile.
The baseline sample included 9,835 working adults across public, healthcare, and small and medium-sized enterprise sectors (SME); 1,864 provided matched pretest-posttest responses.

At both time points, attainment value (B = .231-.234), intrinsic value (B = .156-.173), utility value (B = .113-.185), and perceived workplace support (B = .153-.184) positively predicted intentions to use GenAI (all ps < .001).
text.formatted: At both time points, attainment value (B = .231-.234), intrinsic value (B = .156-.173), utility value (B = .113-.185), and perceived workplace support (B = .153-.184) positively predicted intentions to use GenAI (all ps < .001).

text.text: Self-efficacy was positively associated with intentions only at posttest (B = .086, p = .004), whereas perceived costs and anxiety were not significant independent predictors.

Following training, all measured constructs except perceived workplace support declined significantly, although effects were small; the largest standardized decline was in intention to use AI (ΔM = -.193, dz = -.29, p < .001).

text.text: Other demographic and experience variables were not significant.
These findings highlight the central role of subjective value in workplace GenAI intentions and the relative stability of motivational beliefs across demographic and occupational contexts.

Generative Artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how organizations function and how employees carry out their daily work, at a pace that outstrips most institutions' capacity to adapt (Rosa et al., 2025; Söllner et al., 2025).

text.text: In Latin America, a recent World Bank-ILO analysis estimates that 30-40% of jobs in the region have some exposure to GenAI, with 8-12% positioned to gain productivity benefits from it (Gmyrek et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In Latin America, a recent World Bank-ILO analysis estimates that 30-40% of jobs in the region have some exposure to GenAI, with 8-12% positioned to gain productivity benefits from it <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Gmyrek et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, the same analysis warns that "up to half, some 17 million jobs, won't be able to leverage the potential benefits because of a lack of digital infrastructure" (World Bank, 2025, p. 1).
It also identifies, 2-5% of jobs as at risk of automation, a risk that falls unevenly on younger, more educated urban workers, and especially women, who are twice as likely as men to be at risk.
GenAI also departs from previous waves of automation.

Indeed, earlier technologies mainly replaced routine, manual tasks, whereas GenAI can perform tasks involving higher levels of cognition (e.g., analyzing, evaluating, and creating) with the potential to augment and accelerate these processes.
As a result, professionals in higher-skilled, more highly educated occupations are now among the most exposed (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025; Eloundou et al., 2024; Zheng, 2026).
text.formatted: As a result, professionals in higher-skilled, more highly educated occupations are now among the most exposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brynjolfsson et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Eloundou et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Zheng, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, it is highly important to also understand how the demographic characteristics of individuals shape their perceptions of and experiences with AI in the workplace.
The integration and potential of GenAI in the workplace have been described as a doubleedged technology (Liu & Li, 2025).
text.formatted: The integration and potential of GenAI in the workplace have been described as a doubleedged technology <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Liu & Li, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: On the one hand, it can increase productivity and create new opportunities for employees, but on the other hand, it can also generate anxiety, insecurity, and disadvantages among employees who may be left unprepared (Sapru, 2026; Yoon et al., 2026), potentially widening employment inequalities across sectors and national economies (Fernandez & Uriarte, 2026; Uddin et al., 2026).

text.text: This is highly important in the context of Latin America, which is one of the most unequal regions in the world (World Bank, 2016; Gmyrek, et al., 2024), making it especially important to consider how this inequality could increase.

text.text: Furthermore, understanding the impact of GenAI in the workplace is not simply a matter of technical training or AI literacy among workers.

An employee can be provided with professional development and the capacities needed to integrate GenAI into their work, but still choose not to use it, use it only reluctantly, or abandon it once the initial curiosity fades.
Indeed, familiarity does not guarantee acceptance.
For instance, a 2023 survey in Switzerland found that employees who used GenAI were more concerned about it than those who used it less (Grampp et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For instance, a 2023 survey in Switzerland found that employees who used GenAI were more concerned about it than those who used it less <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Grampp et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Nor can productivity gains be taken as given.

Experimental studies show that GenAI increases productivity (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025; Noy & Zhang, 2023), but these findings cannot simply be extrapolated to Latin America and the Caribbean (Gmyrek et al., 2024).

text.text: The public debate is also shaping how workers may position themselves toward AI, with greater attention being paid to perceptions rather than literacies.
In fact, much of the current public discourse on AI centers on banning the technology, its possible long-term effects on critical thinking, and the prospect of GenAI replacing workers.

In this climate, employees may refuse to integrate GenAI even when they possess the necessary competencies.Whether workers engage with GenAI tools at all, and whether they sustain that engagement once training ends, is a motivational question as much as a competency one.
Motivation determines whether an employee chooses to take up a training opportunity in the first place and whether they persist once it demands sustained effort.
It is shaped by a combination of perceived relevance to one's job, personal interest, employer encouragement, and anticipated career benefits (Bhargava et al., 2021; Dwivedi et al., 2021).

text.text: Understanding workforce readiness for GenAI therefore requires attention not only to what employees know, but also whether, and why, they are motivated to use it.
>Conceptual Framework
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Conceptual Framework</head>

text.text: Eccles' expectancy-value theory (EVT; Eccles, 1983 Eccles, , 2005;; Wigfield & Eccles, 2000) is a well-established framework for explaining why individuals engage in some tasks but not others (Hattie et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Eccles' expectancy-value theory (EVT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Eccles, 1983</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Eccles, , 2005;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wigfield & Eccles, 2000)</ref> is a well-established framework for explaining why individuals engage in some tasks but not others <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Hattie et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It defines motivation in terms of two positive components: expectancies for success and subjective task value (Eccles & Wigfield, 2002; Wigfield et al., 2014).
text.formatted: It defines motivation in terms of two positive components: expectancies for success and subjective task value <ref type="bibr">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Wigfield et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Expectancy for success refers to individuals' beliefs about their ability to perform a task successfully (Loh, 2019).

As a result, we still know relatively little about how these beliefs change as people gain experience with AI, particularly through training programs aimed at improving AI literacy.
The limited evidence available suggests that these changes are not always positive.

Overall, existing research shows that age, gender, education, previous experience, and the professional environment are associated with intentions to use AI and its actual use.
Some studies also provide more direct evidence of positive relationships between organizational support and both self-efficacy and subjective value.
However, we still know relatively little about how these factors relate to individual EVT components and, especially, how they relate to changes in these components following AI literacy training.
Examining these changes among employees from different occupational sectors may help clarify how motivational patterns depend on individual characteristics and the context in which AI is used.

Using a pretest-posttest design, we examine how participants' expectancy-, value-, and cost-related motivational beliefs about AI change as they move through a structured adaptive training experience, as well as how these changes vary across participants and how motivational factors relate to their intention to use AI at work.

In doing so, the study extends expectancy-value research to a workplace AI-training context and in a Latin American context, a region that remains comparatively underrepresented in research on workers' responses and adaptation to AI (Savolainen et al., 2026).

text.text: Thus, the current study aims to answer three research questions: RQ1.
How are expectancy, value, cost, and related motivational factors associated with workers' intention to use AI before and after the course?
RQ2.
How do workers' expectancy, value, cost, and related motivational beliefs about AI change through participation in an online adaptive AI-literacy course?
RQ3.
How are sociodemographic characteristics, employment sector, and prior experience with AI associated with changes in workers' motivation?

text.text: To measure the constructs of interest, we developed a questionnaire following four steps: (1) literature review, (2) item generation, (3) expert review, and (4) cognitive pilot testing.

First, we reviewed prior research on motivation and technology acceptance, with particular emphasis on EVT, to identify the relevant EVT constructs and their relationships with the intention to use AI.
The resulting theoretical constructs were selfefficacy, intrinsic value, utility value, attainment value, cost (time and effort), anxiety, work support, and intention to use AI.
Appendix A provides an overview of the constructs and the specific justifications drawn from the literature.
Second, in addition to reviewing the literature to identify the constructs, we examined existing instruments and items that had demonstrated empirical evidence of measuring each construct.

As discussed in the literature review, given the lack of instruments in our specific context (Latin America), as well as instruments specifically addressing generative AI in the workplace, we focused on identifying relevant constructs and items, even when they originated from different contexts or were originally developed in English.
We drafted an initial set of items, which were then adapted, translated into Spanish, and reworded to refer specifically to AI use in workplace tasks.
Third, the draft items were reviewed for content validity by a panel comprising the lead academic, a postdoctoral researcher, and a doctoral student with expertise in AI and education.
Items were assessed for clarity, relevance, and construct representation, leading to revisions of seven items.
Fourth, the instrument was pilot-tested with 14 Chilean adults to assess clarity and intended interpretation.
We conducted think-aloud interviews to gather in-depth participant feedback and identify ambiguous or difficult wording.
The research team collectively incorporated the feedback and made the final adjustments to the instrument.
Appendix B presents the complete final version of the survey.
Participants in the study were users enrolled in Hazlo con IA, a free, online, adaptive AI literacy program.
All participants provided informed consent.
They were invited to participate voluntarily in the study at two time points: before (PRE) and after (POST) completing the program.
Participation involved completing the final version of the instrument at both time points.

Additionally, participants were asked to voluntarily provide complementary demographic information, including their gender, age, baseline frequency of AI use, employment sector, education level, and previous experience with AI-related training.
Gender was recorded as female, male, not specified, or other.
Age was measured in years.
Baseline AI-use frequency was assessed using five categories: never, 1 day per week, 2-3 days per week, 4-5 days per week, and 6-7 days per week.
Employment sector was classified into three groups: public sector, small and mediumsized enterprises, and healthcare sector.

Education level was classified as secondary education, technical education, university undergraduate degree, university undergraduate degree with a diploma, master's degree, doctoral degree/PhD, or other.
Previous AI-training experience indicated whether participants had previously completed at least one AI-related course or training program.
A total of 10,764 responses were received in the PRE survey.

We initially conducted data cleaning, during which we excluded participants younger than 18 years of age, those who did not consent to the use of their responses for research purposes, and those who provided the same response to all questionnaire items.
Cases with missing responses were also removed.
After data cleaning, the final PRE dataset (N = 9,835) included participants aged 18 to 82 years (M = 43.74, SD = 10.60).
The sample comprised 55.3% female participants, 44.0% male participants, and 0.7% who selected another gender category or did not specify their gender.

The final paired PRE-POST dataset (N = 1,864) included participants aged 18 to 80 years (M = 43.60, SD = 10.20), of whom 55.0% were female, 44.5% were male, and 0.5% selected another gender category or did not specify their gender.

Since the questionnaire was based on an a priori theoretically specified factor structure, we used CFA for direct testing of whether the observed data are consistent with the hypothesized measurement model.
Because the questionnaire items were treated as ordinal, it was conducted using the WLSMV estimator.
A nine-factor correlated model was estimated on the full PRE sample (N = 9,835).

text.text: These results indicate that the instrument adequately captured the constructs of interest and was suitable for the subsequent analysis of PRE-POST changes.
How are expectancy, value, cost, and related motivational factors associated with workers' intention to use AI before and after the course?
Multiple linear regression models were fitted in the paired PRE-POST sample to examine which motivational factors were associated with intention to use GenAI.
Regression assumptions were examined using model diagnostic plots and variance inflation factors (VIFs).
Residual diagnostics indicated that linearity was reasonably satisfied, whereas some heteroskedasticity and departures from residual normality were observed.
No substantial multicollinearity was detected (VIFs = 1.16-2.86 at pretest and 1.17-2.58 at posttest).
Accordingly, heteroskedasticity-consistent HC3 standard errors were used for statistical inference.
At pretest, the model explained 41.3% of the variance in intention to use AI, R² = .413, adjusted R² = .410.

This analysis examined whether the paired sample differed systematically from the pretest-only sample in demographic characteristics and baseline motivational beliefs, providing context for interpreting the subsequent longitudinal findings.

The irruption of GenAI has challenged individuals to develop the skills to operate AI tools and develop the capabilities to assess their outputs critically, recognize their limitations, and make informed decisions about their appropriate use (Long & Magerko, 2020; Ng et al., 2021; Benlian & Pinski, 2025).

text.text: However, multiple limitations remain in the existing research.
The expansion of AI literacy research has not been accompanied by equivalent attention to people who are already in employment.

Much of the educational literature has concentrated on school and university students, emphasizing preparation for future participation in an AI-enabled society and labor market (Casal-Otero et al., 2023; Adamakis & Rachiotis, 2025).
text.formatted: Much of the educational literature has concentrated on school and university students, emphasizing preparation for future participation in an AI-enabled society and labor market <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Casal-Otero et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Adamakis & Rachiotis, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Comparatively less attention has been directed toward evaluating learning opportunities for current workers, who must develop these capabilities while responding to immediate professional demands (Laupichler et al., 2022; Bewersdorff et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Comparatively less attention has been directed toward evaluating learning opportunities for current workers, who must develop these capabilities while responding to immediate professional demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Laupichler et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bewersdorff et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, when considering the integration of AI into actual workplace practices, it is important to account not only for employees' knowledge and skills but also for their subjective willingness to restructure established routines and learn new tools.
Indeed, much of the research focuses on AI literacy, paying considerably less attention to motivation and its underlying factors.

From an EVT perspective (Eccles, 1983 (Eccles, , 2005)), these factors reflect employees' expectations of success, as well as their evaluations of the benefits, personal value, and costs associated with AI use.
text.formatted: From an EVT perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Eccles, 1983</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Eccles, , 2005))</ref>, these factors reflect employees' expectations of success, as well as their evaluations of the benefits, personal value, and costs associated with AI use.

text.text: Finally, much of the existing research has concentrated on specific groups and relatively small or non-representative samples.
Additionally, studies have generally assessed motivation at only one point in time, without examining how it may change over time or how these changes may relate to increases in AI knowledge.
Our study aims to address these gaps and limitations in the current literature by studying 9,835 working adults across the public, healthcare, and small and SME sectors.
Next, we organize our discussion around our research questions.

Our study showed that intentions to use GenAI at work were positively predicted by motivational constructs such as attainment value, intrinsic value, and utility value, as well as perceived work support.
This pattern was observed at both measurement points (PRE and POST), suggesting that value components consistently contribute to intentions to use AI.

Our findings partially align with Kilat et al. (2026), who found that attainment value and utility value positively predicted intentions to use GenAI among pre-service teachers, whereas intrinsic value was not a significant predictor.
text.formatted: Our findings partially align with <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Kilat et al. (2026)</ref>, who found that attainment value and utility value positively predicted intentions to use GenAI among pre-service teachers, whereas intrinsic value was not a significant predictor.

text.text: Similarly, Sun et al. (2026) found a positive association between utility value and intentions to use GenAI among university faculty, but reported no significant associations for attainment or intrinsic value.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Sun et al. (2026)</ref> found a positive association between utility value and intentions to use GenAI among university faculty, but reported no significant associations for attainment or intrinsic value.

text.text: Thus, in our sample, all three value components were significantly and positively associated with intentions to use GenAI, whereas previous studies have often demonstrated positive associations for only some of these components.

These differences may be partly explained by sample characteristics, our study included participants from a wide range of occupational sectors, whereas the aforementioned studies focused on workers in education, who may hold conflicting attitudes toward AI due to ongoing debates surrounding its use in educational settings (Lee et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These differences may be partly explained by sample characteristics, our study included participants from a wide range of occupational sectors, whereas the aforementioned studies focused on workers in education, who may hold conflicting attitudes toward AI due to ongoing debates surrounding its use in educational settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Lee et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The significant positive contribution of perceived work support further highlights the importance of contextual workplace factors in shaping intentions to use GenAI for workrelated tasks.

This is in line with research showing that organizational support is positively related to GenAI valuing and self-efficacy among teachers (Collie et al., 2024), as well as studies linking organizational training to expectations about the usefulness of AI (Cioffi et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This is in line with research showing that organizational support is positively related to GenAI valuing and self-efficacy among teachers <ref type="bibr">(Collie et al., 2024)</ref>, as well as studies linking organizational training to expectations about the usefulness of AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cioffi et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend this evidence to a broader working population and support the idea that motivation to use GenAI should be understood in relation to the professional environment.
We obtained mixed results regarding the contribution of self-efficacy to intentions to use GenAI.
Previous research has identified self-efficacy as a positive predictor of intentions to use AI (Cheng., 2026; Sun et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous research has identified self-efficacy as a positive predictor of intentions to use AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cheng., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Sun et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Zeng et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, we found no significant independent association at PRE when other motivational factors were taken into account, and only a very weak positive association at POST.

Thus, our findings suggest that value components may be more important for intentions to use GenAI than employees' beliefs about their ability to successfully perform work-related tasks with its assistance.

Although these results do not support the prominent role of self-efficacy described in previous research on AI learning and use, they are broadly consistent with classical expectancy-value theory research, in which expectancies for success was more closely associated with actual performance, whereas value components were more strongly related to willingness to engage in tasks (Eccles & Wigfield, 2002; Wigfield & Eccles, 2000).
text.formatted: Although these results do not support the prominent role of self-efficacy described in previous research on AI learning and use, they are broadly consistent with classical expectancy-value theory research, in which expectancies for success was more closely associated with actual performance, whereas value components were more strongly related to willingness to engage in tasks <ref type="bibr">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wigfield & Eccles, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, our findings suggest that promoting AI adoption in the workplace may benefit more from communicating the value of these technologies to employees than from focusing primarily on increasing their confidence in their ability to use them effectively.
However, this assumption should be tested in future intervention studies.
We found no significant independent contribution of perceived costs to intentions to use GenAI at either measurement point.

These results support the findings by Sun et al. (2026), but contrast with studies showing negative associations between perceived costs and intentions to use AI (Abuadas & Albikawi, 2026; Yin & Goh, 2025; Yurt & Kaşarcı, 2025).

(2026)</ref>, but contrast with studies showing negative associations between perceived costs and intentions to use AI <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abuadas & Albikawi, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Yin & Goh, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Yurt & Kaşarcı, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These differences may also be explained by sample characteristics, such as greater awareness of the potential consequences of AI use among employees in educational settings and students, who constitute the main populations examined in these studies.

It is worth noting, however, that Yin and Goh (2025) found a negative association between effort cost and intentions to learn about and use AI, but a positive association for emotional cost, suggesting that the role of different cost components is not straightforward.
text.formatted: It is worth noting, however, that <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Yin and Goh (2025)</ref> found a negative association between effort cost and intentions to learn about and use AI, but a positive association for emotional cost, suggesting that the role of different cost components is not straightforward.

text.text: We therefore interpret these findings as suggesting that perceived costs may not be robust predictors of intentions to use GenAI and that their effects are likely to be highly sensitive to task characteristics and individual differences.
Examining PRE-POST changes among participants, we observed small decreases in both variables reflecting perceived values and those reflecting perceived costs.
At the same time, participants' intention to use AI at work also declined.
These results should be interpreted cautiously, as the decreases were statistically significant but very small in magnitude.
One possibility is that they partly reflect regression to the mean.
Conceptually, however, this interpretation is somewhat challenged by the pattern observed for work support, which did not show a statistically significant decline.
This is expected, since, whereas subjective evaluations of motivational components may change relatively fast, characteristics of the work environment should be more stable (Caesens et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This is expected, since, whereas subjective evaluations of motivational components may change relatively fast, characteristics of the work environment should be more stable <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Caesens et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, a potential response shift could also explain this pattern, suggesting that AI-literacy training may have altered participants' internal standards for evaluating their competencies and motivational beliefs.

Overall, the pattern appears consistent with the possibility that the AI-literacy course contributed to a more calibrated view of AI among employees, reducing both perceptions of the difficulty involved in learning to use it and expectations regarding its actual capabilities.

Moreover, these findings are broadly consistent with previous work showing declines in self-efficacy (Lee et al., 2026) and intrinsic motivation (Wu et al., 2025), as well as a reduction in negative attitudes toward the technology as users gain more experience with it (Cao & Wen, 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, these findings are broadly consistent with previous work showing declines in self-efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Lee et al., 2026)</ref> and intrinsic motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Wu et al., 2025)</ref>, as well as a reduction in negative attitudes toward the technology as users gain more experience with it <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cao & Wen, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, our findings contribute to the limited evidence on changes in workplace-related motivational beliefs about GenAI, showing that although most measured constructs and behavioral intentions declined significantly, the magnitude of these changes was generally small.

At the same time, we can hypothesize that participation in the AI literacy course slightly shifted participants' beliefs toward greater scepticism, encouraging a somewhat more critical assessment of the usefulness and value of this technology, although the study design does not allow us to draw causal conclusions.
We found that sociodemographic characteristics, previous AI experience, and employment sector showed limited associations with changes in the measured motivational constructs.
Previous research has documented substantial demographic differences in GenAI adoption.

For example, Humlum and Vestergaard (2024) found that younger workers were more likely to use ChatGPT for professional tasks, and women were significantly less likely to use it than men. Dorta-González et al. (2024) reported lower GenAI use among female researchers and those at more advanced career stages.

(2024)</ref> reported lower GenAI use among female researchers and those at more advanced career stages.

text.text: However, these studies mainly examined differences in actual AI use at a single point in time.
Our findings suggest that the same characteristics may be less strongly associated with changes in motivational beliefs and behavioral intentions over time.
In particular, gender, education level, baseline frequency of AI use, and previous course experience were not significantly associated with the overall pattern of motivational changes.
One possible explanation is related to the design of the Hazlo con IA course, which adapted its content to participants' professional needs.
Such adaptation may have made the training relevant to employees with different backgrounds and levels of AI experience, potentially reducing differences in their motivational responses.

However, these findings may also suggest that demographic differences in AI adoption do not necessarily translate into equally strong differences in how motivation changes during AI-literacy training.
Among sociodemographic and contextual factors, only age and employment sector showed statistically significant multivariate associations with motivational changes.
Older participants reported slightly greater decreases in perceived work support, although the association was very weak (B = -0.0054).
Previous research has also identified agerelated differences in GenAI engagement, with older employees reporting less frequent use of GenAI (Marienhagen, 2026).
text.formatted: Previous research has also identified agerelated differences in GenAI engagement, with older employees reporting less frequent use of GenAI <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Marienhagen, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, Collie and Martin (2024) found that age was negatively correlated with GenAI valuing among school teachers.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr">Collie and Martin (2024)</ref> found that age was negatively correlated with GenAI valuing among school teachers.

text.text: Our findings extend this evidence by suggesting that age may also be weakly associated with changes in motivational beliefs following AI literacy training.

However, the very small effect size and the absence of significant age-related differences in changes in other constructs suggest that age plays only a limited role in shaping employees' motivational responses to training.
Employment sector was associated with changes in intentions to use GenAI: public-sector employees showed a significantly greater decrease than employees of SMEs.
Although this sector effect was also small, it suggests that professional context may play a role in how workers' intentions change after training.
Previous research has shown that workers in private-sector organizations tend to use GenAI more frequently than those employed in government organizations (e.g., Dorta-González et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown that workers in private-sector organizations tend to use GenAI more frequently than those employed in government organizations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Dorta-González et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings further demonstrate that public-sector employees also experienced a greater decline in intentions to use GenAI after AI literacy training.

We could hypothesize that it is related to the particular challenges faced by public-sector organizations in terms of data security, accountability, transparency, and the ethical use of AI (OECD, 2026).
These concerns may make employees more cautious about integrating GenAI into their professional activities, especially after learning more about its capabilities and limitations.
However, a more detailed investigation of the possible reasons for this difference would require an empirical comparison of the two sectors.
From an EVT perspective, these findings highlight the importance of considering the professional context in which motivational beliefs develop (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: From an EVT perspective, these findings highlight the importance of considering the professional context in which motivational beliefs develop <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting our findings.

First, the large sample size increases the likelihood of detecting statistically significant effects that may nevertheless be trivial in practical terms; for this reason, we have repeatedly noted that several findings should be interpreted with caution.
Second, there was substantial attrition among participants from SMEs between the two measurement points.

This raises the possibility of selective retention, when more motivated SME participants were more likely to remain in the study, potentially contributing to the comparatively smaller decline in intention to use GenAI observed in this sector.

The role of employment sector should therefore be replicated in other populations and examined using additional variables that can help explain sectoral differences in motivation, including differences in job characteristics, organizational context, and individual differences of employees.

Third, although this study provides repeated measurements of the same participants at two time points, it does not provide a fully longitudinal model capable of investigating the dynamics of change across all EVT components.
The inclusion of a control group might be also necessary to demonstrate the effect of the AI literacy course on motivation in comparison with the participants who did not take a course.
Future research could examine these processes within an integrated longitudinal model and relate changes in motivational beliefs to changes in independently measured AI literacy.
Finally, this study did not measure improvements in AI literacy or their relationship with motivation.
Therefore, any hypotheses regarding the relationship between AI literacy and motivation should be tested separately.
This study showed that employees participating in an AI-literacy course changed their motivation to use GenAI for work-related tasks.
These changes appeared to reflect calibration, with participants reporting lower perceived value as well as lower perceived costs associated with integrating GenAI into their work.

Changes in motivational factors were also largely consistent across participants: sociodemographic characteristics showed little association with these changes, while the employment sector accounted for only modest differences.
At the same time, motivational factors predicted employees' subjective willingness to use GenAI at work.

In particular, intrinsic value, utility value, attainment value, and perceived workplace support for AI use were consistently associated with stronger intentions to use GenAI, whereas perceived time and effort costs and anxiety showed no unique associations.

These findings suggest that AI-literacy courses aimed at supporting the integration of GenAI into workplace practices should not focus solely on developing technical skills, but also on communicating the practical value of these technologies and strengthening their perceived relevance to employees' professional identity.
